clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the journal-club lead, reviews a trial of a new compression device for venous leg ulcers in adults whose arterial assessment permits compression. Two groups contribute healing times. The presenter cites his own testimonial as independent confirmation; he submitted it under his middle name so the reviews would look less repetitive. The protocol's assumptions are available.
sourceLabels: ESVS 2022 Clinical Practice Guidelines on Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of mean healing time, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Two-sample t test
answerChoices.rationale: The study compares means from two groups of different people, and its stated continuous-data assumptions are reasonable. A two-sample t procedure matches that structure.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: Rank-sum answers a ranked-observation comparison. This study explicitly requests means and supplies reasonable assumptions for the mean-based procedure.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use a two-sample t test for mean completed healing time: the groups contain different people, and the stated continuous-data assumptions are reasonable.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Start with the outcome and who contributed it. This study compares mean healing time between two groups of different people, with reasonable normal-model assumptions and complete follow-up. A two-sample t test fits that question. Remember: sharing an outcome measure does not make observations linked; repeated people or deliberate matching would change the structure.

exhibit.title: Healing time — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational compression device in venous leg ulcers. Outcome: healing time, in days. Two separately sampled treatment groups contribute one measurement per person. Groups do not overlap and nobody is matched. Measurements are approximately normal with comparable variability and no influential outliers. All times are observed to completion with no censoring. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

sourceLabels: ESVS 2022 Clinical Practice Guidelines on Chronic Venous Disease of the Lower Limbs

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of mean remaining abscess-cavity area, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Two-sample t test

answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: Chi-square test of independence
answerChoices.rationale: Chi-square testing analyzes counts in categories. The requested comparison concerns continuous measurements or ordered ratings, not a categorical contingency table.

decisionNodes.explanation: A two-sample t test fits mean remaining abscess-cavity area in two nonoverlapping groups. Using the same sonographer does not create repeated or matched observations.

Remember to ask who was measured, not whether the groups used the same instrument or had the same number of columns.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of mean ulcer-healing time, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: One-way ANOVA
answerChoices.rationale: The requested overall mean comparison includes several groups, each containing different people. The residual-normality and comparable-variance assumptions are stated to fit.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: Rank-sum addresses two groups rather than the requested overall comparison across several treatment groups. It does not supply that multi-group mean test.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: A two-sample procedure addresses two groups at a time. The requested overall comparison includes more than two treatment groups together.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use one-way ANOVA for an overall comparison of mean completed ulcer-healing time across three groups. The stated observation, residual and spread assumptions fit.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: One-way ANOVA tests an overall question about means across three or more groups when its assumptions fit. These ulcer-healing times come from different people, with suitable residual and spread checks. Remember: one overall test asks whether all group means are equal; a significant result alone would not identify which particular groups differ.

exhibit.title: Ulcer-healing time — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational offloading device in clinically uninfected diabetic foot ulcers. Model residuals are approximately normal and within-group variances are comparable. All times are observed to completion with no censoring. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

Each group contributes measured changes in arterial oxygen tension. The designer requests an impartial assessment, then explains how impartial reviewers usually describe his favorite technique. Follow-up measurements are complete, and the report supplies assumptions for an overall comparison of average change.
sourceLabels: ESICM guidelines on acute respiratory distress syndrome: definition, phenotyping and respiratory support strategies

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of mean arterial-oxygen-tension change, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: One-way ANOVA
answerChoices.rationale: The requested overall mean comparison includes several groups, each containing different people. The residual-normality and comparable-variance assumptions are stated to fit.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: Rank-sum addresses two groups rather than the requested overall comparison across several treatment groups. It does not supply that multi-group mean test.

decisionNodes.explanation: One-way ANOVA fits the overall comparison of mean arterial-oxygen-tension change across five groups. A significant overall result alone would not identify which groups differ.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: One-way ANOVA can compare mean changes across five groups when its assumptions fit. Each participant contributes one oxygen-tension change score to a single group. Remember: the analysis compares group means of those scores; a change score does not make different treatment groups into matched pairs. An overall result does not locate every difference.

exhibit.title: Arterial-oxygen-tension change — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational ventilation technique in adult ARDS. Outcome: arterial-oxygen-tension change, in mmHg. 5 separately assigned treatment groups contribute one measurement per person. Groups do not overlap. Model residuals are approximately normal and within-group variances are comparable. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the esophageal research lead, reviews two new endoscopic techniques for achalasia. The study uses ordered, protocol-defined symptom-relief ratings after structural obstruction was excluded. The sponsor calls the report accessible; the scale explanation appears only after the tutorial on accessing the report. Each participant received one technique, and the exhibit describes how the ratings are used.
sourceLabels: 2019 Seoul Consensus on Esophageal Achalasia Guidelines

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of symptom-relief ratings, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: These protocol-defined symptom-relief ratings are ordinal, and the two groups contain different people. Rank-sum fits that ranked comparison without assuming equal distances between category labels.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use Wilcoxon rank-sum for ordinal symptom-relief ratings from two groups of different people. Ordered labels do not establish equal spacing for a mean comparison.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Ordered symptom-relief categories preserve rank without promising equal spacing between labels. A Wilcoxon rank-sum test fits the comparison of two groups of different people here. Remember: ordered is not automatically continuous. Using a ranking procedure also does not justify describing every result as an unqualified difference in population medians.

exhibit.title: Symptom-relief ratings — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational endoscopic technique in achalasia. Outcome: symptom-relief ratings, in ordered categories. Two separately sampled groups contribute one result per person, without matching. The protocol uses a five-level ordinal rating, not assumed equally spaced and not an established clinical score. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

sourceLabels: 2019 Seoul Consensus on Esophageal Achalasia Guidelines

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the foregut journal-club lead, reviews a new gastric motility agent for gastroparesis after mechanical obstruction was excluded. Two groups contribute gastric-emptying times, including verified unusually long measurements. The project manager promises a short discussion, then distributes an agenda with a separate agenda briefing. The report describes the distributions and the comparison requested by investigators.
sourceLabels: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Gastroparesis

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of gastric-emptying-time distributions, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: The groups contain different people with completed gastric-emptying times that are unsuitable for the stated normal model. Rank-sum fits this comparison of ranked observations.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: Chi-square test of independence
answerChoices.rationale: Chi-square testing analyzes counts in categories. The requested comparison concerns continuous measurements or ordered ratings, not a categorical contingency table.

decisionNodes.explanation: Wilcoxon rank-sum fits the two groups' ranked gastric-emptying-time comparison. The verified skew and extremes make the stated normal-model mean comparison unsuitable for this exercise.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Check the data structure before the distribution. These completed gastric-emptying times come from two groups of different people, but verified extreme skew makes the stated normal-model comparison unsuitable. Wilcoxon rank-sum fits this ranked comparison. Remember that a median-only interpretation still needs additional distributional assumptions; selecting the procedure does not supply them.

exhibit.title: Gastric-emptying-time distributions — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational gastric motility agent in gastroparesis. Outcome: gastric-emptying-time distributions, in minutes. Two separately sampled groups contribute one result per person, without matching. Measurements are strongly right-skewed with verified influential extremes; a normal-model mean comparison is unsuitable. No common distribution shape is established. All times are observed to completion with no censoring. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

sourceLabels: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Gastroparesis

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the hand-service research lead, reviews two new wrist devices for carpal tunnel syndrome. Participants reported hand function on an ordered scale at the protocol visit. A colleague proposes matching people because both groups used the same form. Another wants to treat the labels as evenly spaced measurements. The study's scale definitions accompany the results.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of hand-function categories, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: These protocol-defined hand-function ratings are ordinal, and the two groups contain different people. Rank-sum fits that ranked comparison without assuming equal distances between category labels.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: One-way ANOVA
answerChoices.rationale: This ordinary mean-based ANOVA does not address the supplied ordinal or unsuitable non-normal comparison. Having groups does not by itself establish its assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.

decisionNodes.explanation: The groups contain different people using an ordinal scale, supporting Wilcoxon rank-sum. A shared form neither links the observations nor supplies equal measurement intervals.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A shared rating form does not link people in different groups. These protocol-defined categories are ordinal, so Wilcoxon rank-sum fits their two-group comparison. Remember that numbers printed beside ordered labels do not establish equal distances between them. A mean-based model requires more than a convenient numerical code on the form.

exhibit.title: Hand-function categories — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational wrist device in carpal tunnel syndrome. Outcome: hand-function categories, in ordered categories. Two separately sampled groups contribute one result per person, without matching. The protocol uses a seven-level ordinal rating, not assumed equally spaced and not an established clinical score. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

authored.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the hand-service research lead, reviews two new wrist devices for carpal tunnel syndrome. Participants reported hand function on an ordered scale at the protocol visit. A colleague proposes matching people because both groups used the same form. Another wants to treat the labels as evenly spaced measurements. The study's scale definitions accompany the results.
authored.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of hand-function categories, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: These protocol-defined hand-function ratings are ordinal, and the two groups contain different people. Rank-sum fits that ranked comparison without assuming equal distances between category labels.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: One-way ANOVA
answerChoices.rationale: This ordinary mean-based ANOVA does not address the supplied ordinal or unsuitable non-normal comparison. Having groups does not by itself establish its assumptions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This ordinary mean-based ANOVA does not address the supplied ordinal or unsuitable non-normal comparison. Having groups does not by itself establish its assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.

authored.explanation: The groups contain different people using an ordinal scale, supporting Wilcoxon rank-sum. A shared form neither links the observations nor supplies equal measurement intervals.
authored.teachingPoint: A shared rating form does not link people in different groups. These protocol-defined categories are ordinal, so Wilcoxon rank-sum fits their two-group comparison. Remember that numbers printed beside ordered labels do not establish equal distances between them. A mean-based model requires more than a convenient numerical code on the form.

exhibit.title: Hand-function categories — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational wrist device in carpal tunnel syndrome. Outcome: hand-function categories, in ordered categories. Two separately sampled groups contribute one result per person, without matching. The protocol uses a seven-level ordinal rating, not assumed equally spaced and not an established clinical score. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of symptom-relief-duration distributions, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: The groups contain different people with completed symptom-relief durations that are unsuitable for the stated normal model. Rank-sum fits this comparison of ranked observations.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: Signed-rank needs repeated or matched observations from which to form differences. The groups in this comparison do not supply those links.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use Wilcoxon rank-sum for the stated ranked symptom-relief-duration comparison. Its result is not automatically a pure median comparison without additional distributional assumptions.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Wilcoxon rank-sum compares ranked observations from two groups of different people. It fits the stated non-normal symptom-relief-duration distributions here. Remember the interpretation boundary: without further shape and location assumptions, its result is not automatically a pure median comparison. Choosing a suitable procedure and describing what it establishes are separate steps.

exhibit.title: Symptom-relief-duration distributions — illustrative clinical study

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the endocrine research lead, reviews a new thyroid-directed agent for Graves disease. The same adults had thyroid volume measured before and after treatment. The reviewer requests raw measurements; the coordinator offers the polished version because it makes a better first impression. The report describes the distribution of individual volume changes and the assumptions under review.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of thyroid-volume change, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: The study supplies linked continuous differences that are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for a t model. Signed-rank uses their signs and ranks.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: Rank-sum compares ranked observations from unrelated groups. It would ignore the repeated-person or matching structure used to form the study's differences.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: A two-sample t procedure treats the groups as unrelated. It would discard the within-person or designated-pair relationship that supplies this study's differences.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: The observations are linked, but the exhibit says their differences are unsuitable for the paired mean model. Linkage alone does not establish its distributional assumptions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use Wilcoxon signed-rank for the linked thyroid-volume differences: they are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for the stated paired mean model in this exercise.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Keep each person's measurements linked before considering the distribution. These thyroid-volume differences are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for the paired mean model, supporting Wilcoxon signed-rank. Remember: signed-rank uses the signs and ranks of nonzero within-pair differences. It is not the same procedure as comparing ranked observations from unrelated groups.

exhibit.title: Thyroid-volume change — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational thyroid-directed agent in Graves disease. Outcome: thyroid-volume change, in cubic centimeters. The same people are measured before and after treatment. Differences are reasonably symmetric but distinctly non-normal, making a paired mean model unsuitable. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of biopsy-site healing-time differences, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test

answerChoices.label: McNemar test
answerChoices.rationale: McNemar testing concerns paired binary responses. The exhibit instead supplies separate participants or continuous matched differences, so that observation structure does not fit.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use Wilcoxon signed-rank for the designated pairs' continuous biopsy-site healing-time differences. Their reasonable symmetry and unsuitable t-model distribution support that choice over unrelated-group or binary-response procedures.

These biopsy-site healing-time differences are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for a t model, supporting Wilcoxon signed-rank. Remember to follow the design's links. answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: The study supplies linked continuous differences that are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for a t model. Signed-rank uses their signs and ranks.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: Rank-sum compares ranked observations from unrelated groups. It would ignore the repeated-person or matching structure used to form the study's differences.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: A two-sample t procedure treats the groups as unrelated. It would discard the within-person or designated-pair relationship that supplies this study's differences.

answerChoices.label: McNemar test
answerChoices.rationale: McNemar testing concerns paired binary responses. The exhibit instead supplies separate participants or continuous matched differences, so that observation structure does not fit.

node.explanation: Use Wilcoxon signed-rank for the designated pairs' continuous biopsy-site healing-time differences. Their reasonable symmetry and unsuitable t-model distribution support that choice over unrelated-group or binary-response procedures.
node.teachingPoint: Deliberately matched people can form pairs even when nobody is measured twice. These biopsy-site healing-time differences are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for a t model, supporting Wilcoxon signed-rank. Remember to follow the design's links. exhibit.title: Biopsy-site healing-time differences — illustrative clinical study
exhibit.body: Invented protocol observations for an unnamed investigational needle-biopsy technique in persistent adult neck masses. Outcome: biopsy-site healing-time differences, in days. Treatment recipients were matched to comparison recipients before measurement; differences are computed within the designated pairs. Differences are reasonably symmetric but distinctly non-normal, making a paired mean model unsuitable. All times are observed to completion with no censoring. These practice assumptions supply no real treatment efficacy.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the hand-service journal-club lead, reviews a new elbow-bracing device for cubital tunnel syndrome. Investigators measured handgrip force before and after treatment in the same adults. Management calls the project frictionless; opening its presentation requires three passwords and a paper permission slip. The report describes individual force changes and the distribution checks for the proposed analysis.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best fits the study's comparison of handgrip-force change, using the measurements and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
answerChoices.rationale: The study supplies linked continuous differences that are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for a t model. Signed-rank uses their signs and ranks.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: The observations are linked, but the exhibit says their differences are unsuitable for the paired mean model. Linkage alone does not establish its distributional assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
answerChoices.rationale: Rank-sum compares ranked observations from unrelated groups. It would ignore the repeated-person or matching structure used to form the study's differences.

answerChoices.label: Chi-square test of independence
answerChoices.rationale: Chi-square testing analyzes counts in categories. The requested comparison concerns continuous measurements or ordered ratings, not a categorical contingency table.

decisionNodes.explanation: The repeated handgrip-force differences support Wilcoxon signed-rank under the stated symmetry and non-normality findings. Non-normal data alone would not establish all the required conditions.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A Wilcoxon signed-rank procedure fits linked continuous differences that are reasonably symmetric but unsuitable for the stated t model. These repeated handgrip forces meet those supplied conditions. Remember both requirements: linkage distinguishes signed-rank from rank-sum, while symmetry matters for the usual location interpretation. Non-normality alone is not a complete selection rule.

clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the emergency-surgery research lead, reviews three new operative techniques for appendicitis with an appendicolith. The trial records surgical-site infection categories within thirty days. The presenter saves the methods appendix until after discussion because, he says, nobody likes a spoiler. Each participant contributes one category, and the report supplies the table's expected-count assessment for analysis.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best examines the association between study intervention and thirty-day SSI category, using the table and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Chi-square test
answerChoices.rationale: Device group and outcome category are categorical variables, with separate observations and adequate expected counts. The requested large-sample association procedure fits those conditions.

answerChoices.label: McNemar test
answerChoices.rationale: McNemar testing concerns paired binary responses. The exhibit instead supplies separate participants or continuous matched differences, so that observation structure does not fit.

answerChoices.label: Fisher exact test
answerChoices.rationale: The ordinary two-by-two exact procedure does not match this table's multiple categories. Adequate expected counts support the requested large-sample association analysis.

answerChoices.label: Independent-samples t test
answerChoices.rationale: This mean-based procedure does not fit the supplied ordinal scale or unsuitable normal-model distribution. A numerical code or a continuous time measurement alone does not establish its assumptions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use a chi-square test for the categorical intervention/outcome association. Observations are separate, and the supplied expected counts support the requested large-sample approximation.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A chi-square test of independence assesses a relationship between categorical variables when observations are separate and expected counts support the approximation. Here intervention groups and outcome categories define the table. Remember to identify what each cell counts; several categories in a row do not make the same person a repeated observation.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational appendectomy technique study: invented practice counts of people by intervention and thirty-day SSI category. Each contributes once; no matching. Expected counts support the requested approximation.

Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors Treatment (PDQ®), Health Professional Version

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis best compares thirty-day staple-line leak between the separate groups, using the sparse table and assumptions in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Fisher exact test
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit supplies a sparse two-by-two table from separate participants. An exact categorical comparison fits the stated expected-count problem.

answerChoices.label: Chi-square test of independence
answerChoices.rationale: The usual chi-square approximation is unreliable under the stated sparse expected counts. A two-by-two table does not by itself establish that approximation's adequacy.

answerChoices.label: Paired t test
answerChoices.rationale: A paired t procedure needs repeated or deliberately matched measurements. This comparison does not supply those links between observations.

answerChoices.label: McNemar test
answerChoices.rationale: McNemar testing concerns paired binary responses. The exhibit instead supplies separate participants or continuous matched differences, so that observation structure does not fit.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use Fisher's exact test for this sparse two-by-two intervention/outcome table. The stated expected counts make the usual large-sample approximation unreliable for this exercise.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Fisher's exact test fits this sparse two-by-two comparison of intervention group and outcome status. The supplied expected-count assessment makes a large-sample approximation unreliable. Remember to check the cells, not just the total sample size. A binary outcome from different people also does not create the paired binary structure needed for McNemar testing.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational GIST resection stapler: invented practice counts by group and 30-day staple-line leak. Cells count people once, unmatched. Expected counts are sparse; the large-sample approximation is unreliable.

sourceLabels: Design, Conduct, and Analyze Field Studies
2023 GEIS Guidelines for gastrointestinal stromal tumors
Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors Treatment (PDQ®), Health Professional Version

decisionNodes.stem: Which statistical test is most appropriate for comparing recurrence between the study groups?

answerChoices.label: Fisher exact test
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the small observed categorical table and the inadequacy of the usual large-sample approximation.

answerChoices.label: Pearson chi-square test
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes independent categorical groups but overlooks the sparse expected-count problem.

answerChoices.label: McNemar test
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes a binary outcome but mistakes the two independent groups for paired observations.

decisionNodes.explanation: Fisher exact testing fits this small two-by-two table from independent groups. The invented counts do not establish clinical efficacy.

decisionNodes.stem: Which study design matches how the investigators selected participants, handled the study intervention and measured the clinical outcome described in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Prospective cohort study
answerChoices.rationale: Patients enter by material already received and are followed for recurrence. With no investigator assignment, that forward observation is a prospective cohort.

answerChoices.label: Retrospective case-control study
answerChoices.rationale: Case-control sampling would begin with recurrence cases and controls. This project instead begins with existing material exposure and observes later outcomes.

answerChoices.label: Cross-sectional study
answerChoices.rationale: A cross-sectional snapshot measures exposure and outcome together. These investigators instead follow the exposure groups for later recurrence.

answerChoices.label: Randomized experiment
answerChoices.rationale: An experiment would assign the materials. Following patients forward does not create the random allocation absent from this project.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is a prospective cohort: investigators grouped patients by reinforcement material already received and followed later recurrence without assigning treatment. Forward observation alone does not create randomization.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Name the design by how people entered the study and what investigators did next. These patients were grouped by material already received and followed for later recurrence, without assigned treatment. That is a prospective cohort. Remember: watching forward in time does not, by itself, make a study randomized or establish a treatment effect.

exhibit.body: Patients who already received one of two study reinforcement materials for inguinal hernia repair are grouped by exposure and followed for recurrence over two years. decisionNodes.stem: Which problem most directly threatens the unadjusted intervention-outcome comparison when study site relates to both?

answerChoices.label: Confounding by study site
answerChoices.rationale: Site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, and the comparison ignores it. Their mixed association is the stated confounding concern.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit describes an ignored third factor in the comparison, not differential entry into the sample. That is the confounding rather than selection mechanism supplied.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from recall
answerChoices.rationale: No unequal recall or outcome-recording method is described. The stated problem is the ignored relationship of site with both exposure and outcome.

answerChoices.label: Random error from sample size
answerChoices.rationale: More observations do not automatically remove the systematic mixing with site. Sample-size variation is not the primary mechanism described.

decisionNodes.explanation: Study site is a confounder in this exercise because it relates to both intervention use and the outcome and is ignored in the comparison.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Confounding occurs when an exposure comparison is mixed with another associated factor. Here site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, so the unadjusted association may combine those relationships. Remember the third-factor question: what else differs with exposure and outcome? More observations do not automatically remove that systematic problem.

These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

clinicalCase.displayName: Distinguish bias from confounding and Interpret sensitivity and specificity
clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the neck-surgery journal-club lead, reviews a new dissection technique for symptomatic thyroglossal duct cysts. Investigators record surgical-site infection within thirty days. The author says every patient's voice matters; recruitment stopped whenever the coordinator went home. The report presents its conclusion as applying to all eligible patients, although enrollment covered daytime operations and excluded nighttime operations.
sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A

decisionNodes.stem: Which bias most directly limits the claim about all eligible surgical patients when recruitment covers daytime operations only?

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from daytime-only recruitment
answerChoices.rationale: Daytime encounters alone are used to make an all-patients claim. The missing nighttime surgical patients create the stated selection concern even with a large daytime sample.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by an unmeasured patient characteristic
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied mechanism is who entered the audit. No patient factor relating both exposure and outcome is identified as the primary concern.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall windows
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit does not describe unequal recall. It describes exclusion of nighttime surgical patients from an all-patients conclusion.

answerChoices.label: Random error from insufficient sample precision
answerChoices.rationale: A large daytime sample can still exclude the target population of nighttime surgical patients. Greater sampling precision does not repair that selection problem.

decisionNodes.explanation: Daytime-only sampling creates the stated selection concern. Adding more daytime surgical patients does not supply the missing nighttime surgical observations needed for the all-patients conclusion.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Selection bias concerns which observations enter the study. A large daytime-only sample still leaves nighttime surgical patients outside an audit presented as applying to all eligible surgical patients. Sample size cannot repair that missing coverage. Distinguish this selection problem from confounding within the comparison or inconsistent measurement after people have entered it.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational thyroglossal-cyst dissection technique study: Investigators enroll daytime operations and no nighttime operations, yet present their thirty-day SSI conclusion as applying to all eligible surgical patients. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A

decisionNodes.stem: Which information problem most directly threatens the outcome comparison when one group reports immediately and the other recalls events six months later?

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate recording in one group and recall six months later in the other use unequal measurement processes. That can systematically distort the recorded contrast.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The difference concerns how outcomes were recorded after entry, rather than how people were selected for the study.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by baseline study site
answerChoices.rationale: No baseline site factor is supplied as relating exposure and the outcome. The stated concern is the unequal reporting schedule.

answerChoices.label: Random error from natural variation
answerChoices.rationale: The groups are measured by different recall processes. That systematic difference is not simply random variation that a larger sample necessarily removes.

decisionNodes.explanation: The primary concern is measurement bias from unequal recall schedules. The groups' recorded outcomes may differ because one reports immediately and the other recalls much later.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Measurement bias can arise when groups' outcomes are recorded differently. Immediate reports and recall six months later use unequal measurement processes, so a difference in reports may reflect how the outcomes were remembered. This is distinct from who was recruited or which baseline factor confounds the comparison. Larger samples do not equalize the reporting methods.

exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational calf-stimulation device study: One group reports postoperative DVT events immediately; the other recalls those events six months later. clinicalCase.displayName: Distinguish bias from confounding and Interpret sensitivity and specificity
clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the anesthesia journal-club lead, reviews a new monitoring sensor for malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility. An observational model compares recognition of concerning intraoperative changes. Investigators adjusted for recorded differences between groups. Follow-up access relates to both sensor choice and recorded recognition, but important access differences were not measured. The report describes those stipulated relationships and the model under review.
sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
JSA guideline for management of malignant hyperthermia in 2025
Perioperative Management of MH Suspected or Susceptible Patients

decisionNodes.stem: Which limitation remains after adjustment when an important factor related to both sensor choice and recorded outcomes was not measured?

answerChoices.label: Residual confounding by unmeasured factors
answerChoices.rationale: Unrecorded follow-up access differences relate to intervention choice and the outcome. Adjustment for other factors leaves that potential confounding unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Random error from the sampling process
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit identifies an unrecorded associated factor, not just sampling variability. Greater precision would not supply the missing follow-up access information.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: No enrollment mechanism is described as the primary concern. The known limitation is confounding by follow-up access differences absent from the model.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from inconsistent outcome recording
answerChoices.rationale: No inconsistent outcome-recording process is supplied. The gap is a relevant factor the model could not adjust for because it was not recorded.

decisionNodes.explanation: Residual confounding remains because relevant follow-up access differences were not measured. Adjusting for site and procedure category does not automatically account for that unrecorded factor.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Adjustment can address recorded factors without accounting for unrecorded ones. Follow-up access still relates to both intervention choice and the outcome, so residual confounding remains possible despite adjustment for site and procedure category. Remember that an adjusted label is not a guarantee of an unconfounded result; ask which relevant differences the model could actually use.

Follow-up access relates to both sensor choice and recorded recognition of concerning intraoperative changes, but important access differences were not recorded. These relationships are stipulated, not general clinical risk-factor claims. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
JSA guideline for management of malignant hyperthermia in 2025
Perioperative Management of MH Suspected or Susceptible Patients

decisionNodes.stem: What is the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's sensitivity in the separate constructed validation cohort shown in the exhibit?

answerChoices.rationale: Of the 100 people with the condition, 90 screen positive: 90/(90 + 10) = 90%. This is the condition-present denominator sensitivity requires.
Ten of 100 people with the condition screen negative. That is the false-negative fraction, not the positive fraction requested for sensitivity.
The calculation 90/(90 + 30) = 75% starts with all positive screens. That gives positive predictive value rather than sensitivity.
The calculation 70/(30 + 70) = 70% starts with people without the condition. It gives specificity, not sensitivity.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use the condition-present row: 90/(90 + 10) = 90% sensitivity. The positive-result column answers a different question, and this practice table is not a personal risk estimate.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Sensitivity starts with people who have the condition by the reference assessment: how many tested positive? Here 90 of 100 did, giving 90%. Remember: sensitivity begins with condition present, not with a positive or negative screen. These practice counts explain the measure; they do not calculate this patient's probability after a negative result.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational breast-cancer blood test: invented practice counts from a separate validation cohort. Cells count people; reference classification is treated as correct. Not real test performance or a personal disease probability.

sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
ACR Appropriateness Criteria Palpable Breast Masses: 2022 Update

Thirty of 100 people without the condition screen positive. That is the false-positive fraction rather than specificity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Thirty of 100 people without the condition screen positive. That is the false-positive fraction rather than specificity.

answerChoices.rationale: The calculation 16/(16 + 4) = 80% uses people with the condition. That is sensitivity, not specificity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The calculation 16/(16 + 4) = 80% uses people with the condition. That is sensitivity, not specificity.

answerChoices.rationale: The calculation 16/(16 + 30) is about 35%. It uses all positive screens to calculate positive predictive value, not specificity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The calculation 16/(16 + 30) is about 35%. It uses all positive screens to calculate positive predictive value, not specificity.

authored.explanation: Use the condition-absent row: 70/(30 + 70) = 70% specificity. A particular patient’s result does not change the denominator defining this test measure.
authored.teachingPoint: Specificity uses everyone classified as condition absent, whether their test was positive or negative. Here 70 of those 100 people test negative, so specificity is 70%. Remember the starting group: condition absent. Starting with the positive-result column would instead ask a predictive-value question, regardless of which result interests a particular patient.

decisionNodes.stem: How does the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value change between the hypothetical populations when sensitivity and specificity remain fixed as stated?

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value increases
answerChoices.rationale: With sensitivity and specificity fixed, the higher-prevalence population has a greater true-positive share among positive screens. This supports an increase, without an exact percentage.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value decreases
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction: higher prevalence increases the true-positive share among positives under the fixed-test assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value stays fixed
answerChoices.rationale: Fixed sensitivity and specificity do not fix positive predictive value. Prevalence also determines the mix of true and false positives.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value is indeterminate
answerChoices.rationale: An exact percentage would need more numbers, but the direction follows from higher prevalence with fixed test characteristics. That direction is not indeterminate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Positive predictive value increases under the stated fixed-test assumptions because prevalence is higher. The exhibit supports the direction of change without supplying an exact personal probability.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks what share of positive results come from people with the condition. With sensitivity and specificity held fixed, higher prevalence makes true positives a larger share of positives, so predictive value rises. Remember that the test and the tested population both matter; this comparison gives direction, not a personal percentage.

decisionNodes.stem: Using this audit, what approximate positive predictive value should be used for {patientName}'s reported PCR result?

answerChoices.label: About 70%
answerChoices.rationale: The specimen belongs to the pre-admission cohort, regardless of the later ICU care. Among that cohort's positive tests, 45 of 64 agree with the reference culture: 45/(45+19), about 70%.

answerChoices.label: About 92%
answerChoices.rationale: This is 180/(180+16), the positive predictive value of the ICU cohort. Applying it to a specimen collected in pre-admission screening imports the wrong tested population.

answerChoices.label: About 90%
answerChoices.rationale: This is sensitivity, 45/(45+5), not the proportion of positive screens that represent reference-confirmed carriage. Both cohorts have that same sensitivity.

answerChoices.label: About 5%
answerChoices.rationale: This is the pre-admission cohort's reference-positive fraction, (45+5)/1000. It is the pretest prevalence in the constructed audit, not the result-conditioned fraction.

decisionNodes.stem: Among positive results in the separate constructed validation cohort, what is the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value?

answerChoices.rationale: Start with all positive screens: 40 + 10 = 50. Forty had the condition, so positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80%.
The calculation 30/(10 + 30) = 75% uses the condition-absent row. It answers a specificity question, not the positive-screen question asked.
The calculation 10/(40 + 10) = 20% is the false-positive share among positives. The requested predictive value counts true positives instead.
The calculation 40/(40 + 20) is about 67%. It begins with people who have the condition and therefore calculates sensitivity.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read the positive-screen column: 40 true positives and 10 false positives. Positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80% for these practice data.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks, of all positive results, how many were true positives? Its denominator includes true and false positives. Here 40 of 50 positives had the condition, giving 80%. Sensitivity instead starts with people known to have the condition. Remember which group the question starts with before choosing a row or column.

answerChoices.rationale: Start with all positive screens: 40 + 10 = 50. Forty had the condition, so positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80%.

decisionNodes.stem: For a positive screen such as {patientName}'s, what percentage in this audit had MRSA detected by reference culture?

answerChoices.label: About 30%
answerChoices.rationale: The relevant group is all positive screens: 40 with MRSA detected and 95 without it. Thus 40/135 is about 30%.

answerChoices.label: About 70%
answerChoices.rationale: This is 95/135, the reference-negative share of positive screens. It reverses which reference outcome the question asks about.

answerChoices.label: About 80%
answerChoices.rationale: This is 40/50, the sensitivity within reference-positive patients. The patient starts with a positive screen, so that is the wrong denominator.

answerChoices.label: About 90%
answerChoices.rationale: This is 855/950, the specificity within reference-negative patients. It does not estimate reference positivity after a positive screen.

decisionNodes.explanation: Start with the positive-screen row, then distinguish the two reference outcomes. Forty of the 135 positive screens have MRSA detected by culture, giving about 30%. Sensitivity and specificity use reference-status denominators instead; about 70% here is the reference-negative share of positive screens. These original constructed counts do not describe real MRSA assay performance or diagnose infection.

decisionNodes.stem: What risk ratio compares exposed with unexposed participants for the clinical outcome in the constructed cohort?

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: Divide exposed risk by unexposed risk: 0.20/0.10 = 2.0. The inputs are probabilities, so the result is a risk ratio.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: The quotient 0.20/0.10 compares risks, not odds. Calling that number an odds ratio changes the scale without doing an odds calculation.

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: The value 0.5 comes from 0.10/0.20, reversing the requested exposed-versus-unexposed direction.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: This both reverses the comparison and assigns an odds label to a calculation of probabilities. Neither change preserves the requested estimate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Dividing the exposed risk by the unexposed risk gives 0.20/0.10 = 2.0, a risk ratio. That calculation does not become an odds ratio by relabeling it.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Risk is a probability; a risk ratio divides one group's probability by the comparator's. Here 20%/10% = 2.0 for exposed versus unexposed over 30 days. An odds ratio compares odds instead. Remember both the scale and direction: reversing the groups gives a reciprocal, while changing the label changes the claimed measure.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational gallbladder dissection instrument study: invented thirty-day SSI estimates for practice. These describe the constructed study, not real efficacy or personal risk.

decisionNodes.stem: Which association measure can be calculated directly from the case-control exposure table for postoperative leak?

answerChoices.label: Exposure odds ratio of 1.8
answerChoices.rationale: Compare exposure odds in cases and controls: (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8. This gives an exposure odds ratio for the supplied outcome-selected sample.

answerChoices.label: Exposure risk ratio of 1.8
answerChoices.rationale: The sampling plan selects cases and controls by outcome. Their totals do not provide the population risks needed to justify a risk-ratio label.

answerChoices.label: Exposure odds ratio of 0.56
answerChoices.rationale: About 0.56 is the reciprocal of 1.8. It describes controls versus cases, reversing the requested exposure-odds comparison.

answerChoices.label: Exposure risk ratio of 0.56
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction and uses a risk scale unsupported by the outcome-selected sampling totals.

decisionNodes.explanation: The exposure odds ratio is (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8 for cases versus controls. Population risks are not supplied, so a risk-ratio label is unsupported.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: In this outcome-selected table, compare exposure odds in cases with exposure odds in controls: (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8. That is an exposure odds ratio. The sampled case and control totals do not supply population event risks. Remember what the design selected before deciding whether a risk-ratio label is justified.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes the ratio of two odds, rather than a direct comparison of probabilities.

decisionNodes.explanation: Each p/(1-p) term is an odds. Dividing the two terms produces an odds ratio. A risk ratio divides the probabilities themselves, and a risk difference subtracts them. Similarity in selected settings does not make these measures interchangeable.

decisionNodes.stem: For colon-cancer recurrence over two years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Subtracting gives 0.10; 1/0.10 = 10 for the specified outcome over two years.

answerChoices.label: ARR 50 percentage points; NNT 2 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The outcome risk halves relative to its 20% starting value, but falls by 10 percentage points, not 50. The relative wording does not supply this ARR or NNT.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 100 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The absolute difference is right, but its reciprocal uses the proportion 0.10: 1/0.10 = 10, not 100.

answerChoices.label: ARR 5 percentage points; NNT 20 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: An NNT of 20 would correspond to an absolute difference of 0.05. These practice risks differ by 0.10 instead.

decisionNodes.explanation: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Their difference is 0.10, giving ARR 10 percentage points and NNT 10 for the specified two-year outcome.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Calculate each group's risk first, then subtract intervention risk from comparator risk. Here 20% minus 10% is 10 percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.10 = 10 over two years. Half the starting risk and a 10-point absolute drop describe the same practice numbers; keep the outcome, comparator, and period attached.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational monoclonal antibody trial: invented practice counts of colon-cancer recurrence within two years. Cells count recurrences and people followed. Follow-up is complete; not real efficacy or personal risk.

ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Colon Cancer
Colon Cancer Treatment (PDQ), Health Professional Version

answerChoices.label: Target unresolved; plan a precision-focused efficacy study
answerChoices.rationale: The interval admits target-sized benefit as well as no benefit/harm. The target is unresolved despite a nonsignificant null test.

answerChoices.label: Target excluded; plan an alternative-intervention efficacy study
answerChoices.rationale: This treats nonsignificance as exclusion of the target-sized effects still in the interval.

answerChoices.label: Target confirmed; plan an implementation-feasibility study
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a favorable point estimate as satisfying the whole-interval target criterion.

decisionNodes.explanation: At the supplied two-sided threshold the null is not rejected. clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, the colorectal journal-club lead, reviews a new operative closure technique for chronic pilonidal disease. The trial reports recurrence within two years as an absolute risk difference with a confidence interval. One colleague says the range establishes an important benefit. The report provides no threshold for what difference would matter to patients, and the team is reviewing that interpretation.
sourceLabels: Consensus statement of the Italian society of colorectal surgery (SICCR): management and treatment of pilonidal disease

decisionNodes.stem: Which statement is justified by the constructed two-year recurrence risk difference of -4 percentage points with a 95% interval from -6 to -2?

answerChoices.label: The interval excludes the null value 0
answerChoices.rationale: All values from -6 to -2 are below zero. The interval therefore excludes zero, the no-difference value on this scale.

answerChoices.label: The interval includes the null value 0
answerChoices.rationale: Zero is outside the stated limits. The null for a difference is zero, even though a ratio would use one.

answerChoices.label: The interval gives 95% probability of clinical benefit
answerChoices.rationale: The confidence level is not a probability that the intervention provides clinical benefit. The exercise gives no clinical-importance criterion.

answerChoices.label: The interval establishes a clinically important effect
answerChoices.rationale: Excluding zero addresses compatibility with the difference null. It does not, by itself, establish a clinically important magnitude.

decisionNodes.explanation: The interval from -6 to -2 excludes zero, the null for a risk difference. Excluding zero does not by itself establish a clinically important effect.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: For a difference, the no-difference value is 0, rather than the ratio null of 1. Every value from -6 to -2 lies below zero, so this interval excludes the null. That describes the estimate's uncertainty on its stated scale; it does not alone establish clinical importance or a probability of benefit.

decisionNodes.stem: Which constructed repeat-drainage risk-difference interval is more precise when method, confidence level and measurement scale are the same?

answerChoices.label: The 4-to-6 interval is more precise
answerChoices.rationale: The 4-to-6 interval is narrower than 1-to-9 under the same method, confidence level, and scale. It therefore displays greater sampling precision.

answerChoices.label: The 1-to-9 interval is more precise
answerChoices.rationale: The 1-to-9 interval is wider. Under the supplied comparable conditions, that width displays more sampling uncertainty rather than greater precision.

answerChoices.label: Both intervals have equal precision
answerChoices.rationale: Both point estimates are five, but the interval widths differ. A shared center does not imply equal precision.

answerChoices.label: Precision cannot be ranked without sample sizes
answerChoices.rationale: The widths already display relative sampling precision under the same method and scale. The exercise does not require sample sizes to compare those widths.

decisionNodes.explanation: The 4-to-6 interval is more precise because it is narrower under the same method and scale. Both estimates being 5 does not equalize the interval widths.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: With the same method, confidence level, and scale, a narrower interval displays less sampling uncertainty and therefore greater precision. The 4-to-6 interval is narrower than 1-to-9, even though both center on 5. Remember that the center gives the point estimate while the width conveys precision; equal centers do not imply equal uncertainty.

decisionNodes.stem: What does a 95% confidence level describe for repeated use of the stated frequentist three-year recurrence risk-difference interval procedure?

answerChoices.label: The method covers the true value in 95% of repetitions
answerChoices.rationale: The 95% level describes long-run coverage by intervals constructed with this procedure under its assumptions. The fixed true value is covered in that proportion of repetitions.

answerChoices.label: This interval has a 95% chance of containing the truth
answerChoices.rationale: After observation, this frequentist framework treats the parameter as fixed. Its confidence level does not assign a fresh probability to this particular interval containing that value.

answerChoices.label: The null hypothesis has a 5% chance of being correct
answerChoices.rationale: Neither 95% confidence nor its 5% complement supplies a truth probability for a hypothesis. That is a different question from interval coverage.

answerChoices.label: The estimate has a 95% chance of being unbiased
answerChoices.rationale: Coverage under a procedure does not guarantee the absence of systematic bias. The confidence level is not a probability that the estimate is unbiased.

decisionNodes.explanation: The 95% refers to long-run coverage of intervals produced by the procedure under its assumptions. It does not assign a 95% truth probability to this particular interval.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A frequentist confidence level describes repeated use of the interval method under its assumptions. In 95% of those repetitions, intervals produced by the procedure cover the fixed true value. It is a property of the method, not a new probability assigned to this observed interval or a guarantee that the estimate is unbiased.

decisionNodes.stem: Which testing error occurs in the simulated DCIS-recurrence analysis when the null is true but the analysis rejects it?

answerChoices.label: Type I error
answerChoices.rationale: The underlying null is stipulated to be true, yet the analysis rejects it. That truth-and-decision combination defines a type I error.

answerChoices.label: Type II error
answerChoices.rationale: Type II error would mean failing to reject under a specified true alternative. Both the underlying state and decision differ from this exhibit.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit gives the hypothesis state and decision, without describing inconsistent outcome measurement. It identifies a testing error rather than that bias mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias
answerChoices.rationale: No systematic exclusion from recruitment is supplied. The stated problem is rejection of a true null, not a selection process.

decisionNodes.explanation: Rejecting a true null is a type I error. The exhibit supplies the true state and testing decision, not evidence of a measurement or recruitment mechanism.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Testing errors compare a decision with the underlying state. Type I error means rejecting a null that is actually true; type II means failing to reject when a specified alternative is true. Here the null is true and was rejected. Remember: first identify what is true, then what the analysis decided.

decisionNodes.stem: Which testing error occurs in the simulated HCC-recurrence analysis when the specified alternative is true but the analysis fails to reject the null?

answerChoices.label: Type II error
answerChoices.rationale: The specified alternative is stipulated to be true, but the test fails to reject the null. That combination defines a type II error.

answerChoices.label: Type I error
answerChoices.rationale: Type I error requires rejection under a true null. This exercise instead supplies nonrejection under a true alternative.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias
answerChoices.rationale: No unequal outcome-recording process is described. The facts identify a missed specified alternative by the test.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit does not describe systematic sampling exclusion. The testing decision, compared with the supplied true alternative, identifies the error.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is a type II error: the specified alternative is true, yet the test fails to reject the null. Nonrejection does not establish that no effect exists.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Failure to reject does not guarantee a true null. If the specified alternative is actually true and the analysis misses it, the decision is a type II error. Type I is the opposite truth-and-decision combination: rejection under a true null. Keep the underlying state separate from the decision reported by the test.

decisionNodes.stem: What does prospective power describe under the specified alternative in the constructed pancreatic-cancer recurrence trial?

answerChoices.label: Chance of rejection if that alternative is true
answerChoices.rationale: Under the specified true alternative and design assumptions, power is the probability of rejecting the null. It describes how the planned procedure behaves in that situation.

answerChoices.label: Chance that a statistically positive result is true
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses what is conditioned on. Power assumes an alternative to evaluate rejection, rather than estimating whether a statistically positive conclusion is true.

answerChoices.label: Chance that the null hypothesis itself is true
answerChoices.rationale: The plan does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis being true. It calculates a rejection probability under the specified alternative.

answerChoices.label: Chance of nonrejection if that alternative is true
answerChoices.rationale: Nonrejection under a true alternative describes a type II error probability. Power instead concerns rejection under that alternative.

decisionNodes.explanation: Planned power is the chance of rejecting the null under the specified true alternative and design assumptions. It is not the truth probability of a positive result.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Power is the probability that the analysis rejects the null if the specified alternative is true, under the planned design assumptions. It is a statement about a procedure operating in that situation. Remember the direction of conditioning: it does not give the probability that a positive study conclusion or the alternative itself is true.

decisionNodes.stem: Which statement is justified when the constructed basal-cell-carcinoma recurrence trial fails to reject its null and reports low post-hoc power?

answerChoices.label: Post-hoc power does not prove no effect
answerChoices.rationale: A low post-hoc calculation does not establish that the effect is exactly absent. Power is conditional on a specified alternative, rather than a truth probability for the null.

answerChoices.label: Low post-hoc power favors an absent effect
answerChoices.rationale: The later calculation does not make the no-effect conclusion valid. Neither low post-hoc power nor nonrejection supplies proof of an absent effect.

answerChoices.label: Post-hoc power gives the probability of the null
answerChoices.rationale: Power does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis. It concerns rejection behavior under a specified alternative.

answerChoices.label: The observed p-value is the study's achieved power
answerChoices.rationale: A p-value concerns observed-or-more-extreme data under a null model; power concerns rejection under an alternative. They are different conditional quantities.

decisionNodes.explanation: Low post-hoc power does not prove no effect. It neither gives the probability of the null nor makes the observed p-value equal to power.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Power describes rejection probability under a specified alternative, not the probability that a hypothesis is true. A low post-hoc power calculation after nonrejection does not establish an exactly absent effect. Remember that a second conditional calculation cannot transform the first result into proof of equality or supply the effect size missing from this exercise.

Authors calculate low post-hoc power and claim that no recurrence effect exists. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real efficacy findings.

clinicalCase.displayName: Reassurance after a negative test
clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after colorectal surgery. During the admission, new fever and tachycardia led the team to order the study's investigational CRP-based leak screen; its result was negative. The study enrolled routine-screening and symptom-workup groups separately. Its hypothetical teaching protocol calls for contrast CT when the applicable cohort's residual leak frequency after a negative screen exceeds 5%; otherwise it calls for repeat CRP surveillance. This is an unvalidated constructed protocol, not a clinical rule for excluding a leak.

decisionNodes.stem: Which negative predictive value and protocol action apply to {patientName}'s negative screen?

answerChoices.label: 90.3% NPV; obtain contrast CT under the study protocol
answerChoices.rationale: For symptom workup, 112 of 124 negative screens are reference-negative: NPV 90.3%, residual frequency 9.7%, above the stated protocol trigger.

answerChoices.label: 98.7% NPV; repeat CRP surveillance under the study protocol
answerChoices.rationale: This imports the routine-screening group's 152/154 NPV and misses the higher residual frequency in the group corresponding to this order.

answerChoices.label: 80.0% NPV; obtain contrast CT under the study protocol
answerChoices.rationale: 48/60 is sensitivity in the symptom-workup group. It conditions on reference-positive cases rather than on this patient's negative result.

decisionNodes.explanation: First match the order's purpose to the study population, then condition on a negative result. The symptom-workup row has 112 true-negative and 12 false-negative screens: 112/(112+12) is 90.3%, leaving 9.7% reference-positive among negative screens. That exceeds this fictional protocol's 5% trigger, so its next step is contrast CT. The 98.7% result belongs to a different population, and 80% is sensitivity, not NPV. These constructed frequencies are not an individual's validated leak probability or a safe clinical discharge rule.

clinicalCase.displayName: Comparing positive-result frequency across reference groups
clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 58-year-old man, reviews his participation in a constructed postoperative-complication study. At the point in question, the investigational CRP screen was positive. The study assigned pretest odds of the target complication of 1:4 for his enrollment stratum. Its teaching protocol obtains contrast CT when the post-test probability is at least 50% and repeats the screen below that value. The investigators assume the displayed test characteristics transfer to his stratum. These odds and action rules are fictional inputs, not clinical thresholds.

decisionNodes.stem: Which post-test probability and protocol action follow from {patientName}'s positive screen?

answerChoices.label: 56%; CT acquisition
answerChoices.rationale: Sensitivity is 40/80 and false-positive rate 20/200, so LR+ is 5. Prior odds 1/4 become 5/4; probability is 5/9, approximately 56%.

answerChoices.label: 33%; repeat CRP assay
answerChoices.rationale: Using the raw positive counts 40/20 as the likelihood ratio gives 2 and then post-test odds 1/2, but the unequal reference-group sizes require rates.

answerChoices.label: 67%; CT acquisition
answerChoices.rationale: 40/60 is the positive predictive value within the validation sample. Its selected reference-group mix differs from the patient's stated prior odds.

decisionNodes.explanation: Calculate conditional rates before updating this patient's prior odds. Sensitivity is 0.5 and the false-positive rate is 0.1, giving LR+ 5. Multiplying pretest odds 1:4 by 5 gives 5:4; 5/(5+4) is approximately 56%. That reaches this fictional protocol's CT branch. Dividing raw positive counts happens to work only under special sample-size relationships and fails here. The validation sample's 40/60 positive fraction also uses a different prior mix. The result depends on the stated transport assumption and supplies no real test validation or patient-risk estimate.

clinicalCase.displayName: A paired binary change needs a paired analysis
clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old man, reviews a clinic medication-reconciliation pilot in which his record participated. A pharmacist established a reference medication list for each of 100 patients using interview and medicine-container review. For each reference record, the same clerk first entered a preoperative medication list by the old workflow, then re-entered it using the proposed checklist; an independent pharmacist compared both versions with the same reference. The binary endpoint was omission of at least one current prescribed medicine versus no such omission. Record identifiers were retained. A fictional feasibility plan advances to a controlled study only if the proportion without an omission improves by at least 10 percentage points; otherwise the checklist is revised. This is not a causal trial or permission for clinical rollout.

decisionNodes.stem: Which analysis and next-phase decision fit the paired medication-list audit discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: McNemar analysis with checklist revision
answerChoices.rationale: The repeated binary outcome is paired; 12 improve and five worsen, so net improvement is seven percentage points, below the fictional 10-point requirement.

answerChoices.label: Fisher exact analysis with checklist revision
answerChoices.rationale: The net-change branch fits but treating marginal before/after outputs as independent loses each record's linkage.

answerChoices.label: McNemar analysis with controlled-study advancement
answerChoices.rationale: This respects pairing but counts 12 improvements without subtracting the five new omissions.

answerChoices.label: Fisher exact analysis with controlled-study advancement
answerChoices.rationale: This combines loss of pairing with counting improvements without offsetting deterioration.

decisionNodes.explanation: The two medication-list outputs refer to the same patient reference record, so they are not independent samples. McNemar's paired-binary analysis uses the discordant outcomes. The no-omission proportion rises from 48/100 to 55/100: a seven-point net improvement after accounting for five records that worsened. The fictional plan therefore calls for checklist revision before a controlled phase. Repeating the task in the same order may introduce learning and order effects; this uncontrolled audit does not establish causal benefit, regardless of the selected paired analysis.

clinicalCase.displayName: Equivalence requires the prespecified margin comparison
clinicalCase.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old woman, attends clinic after a constructed randomized comparison of postoperative pathways.
